CONGRANT.TITLE: Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger

PI: Hansheng Lei
Co-PI: Xu Lei, Liyu Zhang, Fitra Khan, Mahmoud Quweider

Motivation and challenges. The Internet of Things (IoT) aims at to build an architecture to integrate a wide variety of devices for computation, sensing, communication, and actuation. This concept is then extended to the Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) that can connect all types of units in the battlefield to enable predictive analytics for intelligent command and control and battlefield services. Considering the complexity of IoBT deployment environment, an edge-cloud architecture is a suitable way to connect IoBT devices. Edge computing datacenters are deployed closer to the physical places where IoBT devices are used, and this allows data to be collected and processed locally. IoBT applications running in different edge computing datacenters only need to interact with each other through the cloud datacenter when necessary. Therefore, this architecture greatly reduces unnecessary communication and latency. Furthermore, the edge-cloud paradigm is also consistent with the design of 5G network, which is believed to be critical for DoD. Systems built on top of an IoBT infrastructure, especially systems involving AI, rely on data collected by IoBT for making support decisions and conducting operations of critical infrastructure. A failure of preserving the integrity of such a system can cause serious consequences. However, there is a lack of end-to-end protection of IoBT and systems built on top of it, especially AI systems, which prevents fully unleashing the potential of IoBT.
The goal. The goal of the proposed efforts is to provide end-to-end protection of key IoBT applications, which is achieved through the following objectives: (i) A novel blockchain architecture that is designed to work with IoBT and able to handle a large number of IoT devices in an efficient manner; (ii) an end-to-end IoBT infrastructure protection mechanism based on the newly proposed blockchain architecture, especially for AI systems built on top of it; and (iii) a prototype implementation of the proposed framework and a testbed environment for benchmarking.
Technical approach. The proposed blockchain based end-to-end IoBT protection solution consists of two major components: (i) A novel blockchain scheme that is integrated with edge-cloud architecture and able to support a large number of IoBT devices; and (ii) an integration of the protection mechanism into the proposed blockchain scheme to guarantee the effectiveness of IoBT applications running in the edge-cloud environment. The novel blockchain scheme consists of multiple edge-blockchains and one cloud-blockchain, where multiple edge-blockchains can support massive number of IoBT devices, and the new protocols proposed herein allow each of the blockchains to verify information stored on other blockchains in an efficient way. This novel blockchain scheme is then leveraged to protect AI systems through two steps: protecting the data collection procedure and protecting the model building procedure, which is usually expensive and hard to verify. Due to the immutability feature of blockchain and our novel stochastic checking mechanism, an adversary cannot compromise the integrity of an AI system without tampering with the majority of the peers of the proposed blockchain system.
Expected results. CONGRANT.TITLE: Center for Army HBCU/MI Research Centers of Excellence: Decentralized Ledger based Forensics Infrastructure
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: 1 Motivation and ChallengesThe proposed research targets 1. Information Science, b. Research Area 2 DigitalForensics.Effective information collection, processing, and utilization play an increasingly important role ina variety of defense applications. As a result, the deployment of information systems becomesubiquitous. While the rich data that is unavailable in the past brings many benefits, it also createsnew challenges for forensics. For instance, it is hard to process the massive data to extractdigital evidence manually, and the complexity of the system brings a larger attack surface to theadversaries.The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) sheds light on the challenges and many successfulapplications have been developed. However, AI is a doubleedgedsword for digital forensics, i.e.,it has also been proved to be a powerful tool to generate fake evidence. Although new methods arealso proposed to combat AIgeneratedfake evidence, the situation is more like a catandmousegame. Furthermore, AIbasedforensics tools also suffer from all types of attacks such as datapoisoning and model poisoning, which can lead the tools to make wrong conclusions. Therefore,there is an urgent need to address these limitations to fully unleash the potential of AI in digitalforensics.2 The GoalThe goal of the decentralized ledger based forensics infrastructure is to protect the authenticity ofdigital evidence collected from different resources and offer the capability of tracing back whenan issue is detected. Instead of focusing on content analysis to detect/prevent malicious digital evidence,the team plans to adopt a different strategy to address the challenge of preserving the authenticityof digital evidence. Specifically, the team will design and develop a forensics infrastructurethat can provide a complete history of the lifecycle of digital evidence and offer the capability totrace back. From the original data collection to intermediate processing results and the final digitalevidence used for decision making, each step is authenticated and recorded in the system. Toachieve this goal, the proposed system should provide the following features: (i) Irreversible evidencerecording. When a record of digital evidence is added to the system, it cannot be removedor modified. (ii) Scalability. Considering the large number of data sources, the system must bescalable to handle all of them in an efficient manner. (iii) Flexible data authentication. Whilearbitrary data manipulation should be prevented, there are also legitimate operations that can be appliedto collected digital evidence (e.g., figure enhancement). Therefore, the system should allowthese operations without compromising the data authentication protection mechanism. (iv) Highresilience. The system will be deployed in a complex and hostile environment so it needs to beresilient against adaptive adversaries, and offer functionalities such as critical information leakagedetection and fault tolerance. (v) Privacy preserving auditing. A third party may occasionally needto check the correctness of digital evidence records managed by the system, but it does not need toknow the contents of the evidence.

CONGRANT.TITLE: TRUSTVILLE: Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Getting students’ interest piqued in a college degree in a STEM field is challenging. However, due to ever increasing pace of technology transformation, the area of computer science is frequently afforded an opportunity to attract students to relatively new areas with visible impact on everyday life and business. Cyber security, a field pervasively touching almost every aspect of modern life, boasts a promise of job growth of 28% from 2016 through 2026 according to BLS. On the other hand, according to ISACA, 84% of organizations believe that only half or fewer of the applicants for security jobs are qualified. This proposal is for enhancing Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on a Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment (TRUSTVILLE). The proposed integrated security lab, which includes Internet of Things (IOT) equipment as well, will be familiarizing students with the state of the art cyber security appliances and software in a realistic environment to give them a competitive edge in the job market for serving to fill the existing gap in cyber security in public and private sectors.

The Computer Science Department at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has been offering courses in cyber security area, however, a formal cyber security track with the required training has not been offered due to lack of hardware and software. The institution has Data, Intelligence and Security (DIS) group, with its own lab space, and prides itself for hosting the first International Conference on Data, Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) in April 2018. Given the current faculty expertise in cyber security, experience in teaching related courses, having a DIS group with its own lab space and the market potential for cyber security jobs, the university is strategically poised for offering a specialized track in cyber security to enhance teaching and research.

Due to the market demand, the hardware and software related with cyber security are expensive, and this proposal is for securing funds to assist the institution’s ongoing efforts to establish a market driven cyber security track supported by a modern cyber security integrated laboratory. Since low traffic volume is encountered in a lab environment, expensive high-performance ASIC based hardware is not needed. However, the updates to the firmware and software of security hardware, and to the software itself could be as frequent as daily, for example, to block vulnerabilities including zero-day worms. Therefore, most of the expense of cyber security integrated lab is not in the hardware, but rather in the annual subscription of the software to keep the lab current.

The cyber security track in computer science will consist of seven computer science courses geared towards cyber security, three criminal justice courses, and a senior cornerstone project in the area of cyber security. All of these courses will incorporate Project Based Learning (PBL) methodology to familiarize the students with industry grade cyber security tools and appliances. The required integrated laboratory will consist of a gamut of cyber security related hardware and software to understand and analyze the weaknesses of systems and procedures and learn how to strengthen security at different levels. The integrated security laboratory will consist of software and hardware such as IoT devices, IPS, IDS, threat hunting, vulnerability management, traffic monitoring, penetration testing, forensics, encryption, network security and endpoint security for both on premise and cloud assets.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Fusing Ultrasound and Vision Processing for Assessing Indurations
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Indurations, such as appearing as a result of PPD or tuberculin test, are assessed using finger feel method largely to measure the size of the swelling. For example, in case of PPD test, if the induration is 10mm or less, then the test is considered to be negative. In case of positive test, the patient needs to go through medication for about a year which in itself can cause side effects whereas the process may have been unnecessary. The proposed project is to build an inexpensive portable instrumentation to provide alternative to subjective testing of indurations, and provide more scientific approach to assessment of indurations.

Indurations have two aspects in general. Firstly, the visual aspect such as the shape of the bump, color/hue, and the size. Secondly, an induration has the feel aspect such as the hardness. Both aspects need to be measured to provide more scientific assessment of an induration.

The visual aspect of an induration will be measured through a stereo imaging system. The feel aspect of an induration will be measured through an ultrasound system. 3D signal processing will be performed on the data acquired from both systems to fuse both systems to produce scientific based assessment of an induration.

The testing will be done on artificial arms with simulated indurations.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: A Deep Dive into FAT-32 Windows File System: A Digital Forensics Perspective
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: The 5th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Abstract— For digital forensics analysts, the file system of a digital computing/storage device is a great source of relevant information that can aid in an investigation or analysis of a case at hand. Therefore, a solid understanding of the file system details and how to identify, extract, analyze, and present the data on a given device becomes crucial to a successful inquiry or investigation. In this paper, we present a detailed overview of the Windows operating systems FAT-32 file system with an emphasis on its importance from a digital forensics perspective. We review the overall technical mechanisms and processes with context and background by which files are organized including data (content) and metadata/attributes, identify fields that are unique to the file system, point out places where data can be hidden or masked, and how data recovery and carving techniques work with the file system. We also conduct a detailed walk through of each filesystem component using low level tools and verify the results with the current major tools of acquisition, recovery and carving of data.

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: Texas Tech University
Texas Tech University
University of Houston

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Proceedings 1st Workshop of Security and Privacy in Artificial Intelligence, ACM
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Recommender systems are widely used in a variety of scenarios, including online shopping, social network, and contents distribution. As users rely more on recommender systems for information retrieval, they also become attractive targets for cyber-attacks. The high-level idea of attacking a recommender system is straightforward. An adversary selects a strategy to inject manipulated data into the database of the recommender system to influence the recommendation results, which is also known as a profile injection attack. Most existing works treat attacking and protection in a static manner, i.e., they only consider the adversary’s behavior when analyzing the influence without considering normal users’ activities. However, most recommender systems have a large number of normal users who also add data to the database, the effects of which are largely ignored when considering the protection of a recommender system. We take normal users’ contributions into consideration and analyze popular attacks against a recommender system. We also propose a general protection framework under this dynamic setting.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Weak Mitoticity of Bounded Disjunctive and Conjunctive Truth-table Autoreducible Sets
INTELLCONT.CONTRACT_NUM: Research supported in part by NSF CCF grant 1218093
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Glaßer et al. (SIAMJCOMP 2008 and TCS 2009)2 proved existence of two sparse sets A and B in EXP, where A is 3-tt (truth-table) polynomial-time autoreducible but not weakly polynomial-time Turing mitotic and B is polynomial-time 2-tt autoreducible but not weakly polynomial-time 2-tt mitotic. We unify and strengthen both of those results by showing that there is a sparse set in EXP that is polynomial-time 2-tt autoreducible but not even weakly polynomial-time Turing mitotic. All these results indicate that polynomial-time autoreducibilities in general do not imply polynomial-time mitoticity at all with the only exceptions of the many-one and 1-tt reductions. On the other hand, however, we proved that every autoreducible set for the polynomial-time bounded disjunctive or conjunctive tt reductions is weakly mitotic for the polynomial-time tt reduction that makes logarithmically many queries only. This shows that autoreducible sets for reductions making more than one query could still be mitotic in some way if they possess certain special properties.

Note: A preliminary version of this paper appears in the proceedings of COCOON'18 (24th International Computing and Combinatorics Conference, 2018).

Abstract— With the advent of cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and mobile computing, CS faculty are continuously revamping the curriculum material to address such burgeoning set of technologies in practical and relatable ways. Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices represent an ideal hardware/software framework that embodies all these technologies through its simple architecture, small form factor (that minimizes the volume and footprint of a desktop computer), and ability to integrate various sensors and actuators that network together and connect to the Cloud. Therefore, one of the strategies of Computer Science Department, to enhance depth of learning concepts, has been to infuse Raspberry Pi (RPi) in computer science courses. From implementing firewalls,intrusion detection systems, scripting, client-server based computing, distributed computing, to interfacing with sensors and actuators, a student is guided to polish concepts taught in a class through RPi Project Based Learning (RPBL). Computer science curriculum already provides breadth of learning. The infusion of RPi in key courses provides depth in targeted concepts. From simply interfacing a switch and a Light Emitting Diode (LED) to getting data from sensors,buffering, and uploading to the cloud, a student already would have touched upon multiple disciplines in computer science. This paper provides a blueprint to infusing RPi in the targeted courses, and how each RPi based project provides depth to a targeted concept.

faculty and staff efforts in creating a sustainable framework for implementing a distributed
campus course delivery that is acceptable by the university/college administration, the
department, the faculty, and most importantly the students. Our experience shows that a
successful framework should address many issues, including: Logistics, Scheduling, Faculty
incentives, IT support, course management system and delivery methods, assessment and student
participation. The paper will present our efforts in each of the above areas, showing that despite
the challenges faced, a distributed delivery system can be successful when the above
issues/factors are adequately addressed. The results from our courses at the graduate and
undergraduate levels show that student assessments don’t show any significant difference across
campuses or based on where the home campus of the faculty is. By presenting our study, we
hope that other institutions who are considering distributed education can benefit from our
experience by adopting best practices while avoiding pitfalls.

We unify and strengthen both of those results by showing that there is a sparse set in EXP that is polynomial-time 2-tt autoreducible but not even weakly polynomial-time Turing mitotic. This shows that autoreducible sets for reductions making more than one query could still be mitotic in some way if they possess certain special properties.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Abstract— Image retrieval systems have been an active area of research for more than thirty years progressively producing improved algorithms that improve performance metrics, operate in different
domains, take advantage of different features extracted from the images to be retrieved, and have different desirable invariance properties. With the ever-growing visual databases of images and videos produced by a myriad of devices comes the challenge of selecting effective features and performing fast retrieval on such databases. In this paper, we incorporate Fourier descriptors (FD) along
with a metric-based balanced indexing tree as a viable solution to DHS (Department of Homeland Security) needs to for quick identification and retrieval of weapon images. The FDs allow a simple but effective
outline feature representation of an object, while the M-tree provide a dynamic, fast, and balanced search over such features. Motivated by looking for applications of interest to DHS, we have created a basic guns and rifles databases that can be used to identify weapons in images and videos extracted from media sources. Our simulations show excellent performance in both representation and fast retrieval
speed.

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: 2018 1st International Conference on Data Intelligence and Security
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: There are different traditional approaches to handling a large number of computers or workstations in a campus setting, ranging from imaging to virtualized environments. The common factor among the traditional approaches is to have a user workstation with a local hard drive (nonvolatile storage), scratchpad volatile memory, a CPU (Central Processing Unit) and connectivity to access resources on the network. This paper presents the use of block streaming, normally used for storage, to serve operating system and applications on-demand over the network to a workstation, also referred to as a client, a client computer, or a client workstation. In order to avoid per seat licensing, an Open Source solution is used, and in order to minimize the field maintenance and meet security privacy constraints, a workstation need not have a permanent storage such as a hard disk drive. A complete blue print, based on performance analyses, is provided to determine the type of network architecture, servers, workstations per server, and minimum workstation configuration, suitable for supporting such a solution. The results of implementing the proposed solution campus wide, supporting more than 450 workstations, are presented as well.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Visualization as Effective Instructional and Learning Tools in the Computer Science Curriculum
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Visualization (the use of images, diagrams, presentations, animations, and video) represents a potentially great aid in teaching and learning, especially in the STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields where abstract complex ideas and concepts are abound. Educators, especially in academia, are always searching for effective pedagogical methodologies to use in the classroom to enhance students’ understanding and retention of key concepts of the subject area they are teaching. With the rapid advancements in software, hardware, networking, computing and storage technologies, including laptops, tablets, smartphones, cloud and distributed computing, the use of multimedia as an effective tool and aid in the classroom has become a standard procedure, rendering obsolete the traditional pure “chalk and talk”. The next natural step to take is to enhance the presented course content through effective multimedia techniques. Of those techniques, visualization and animation have the most potential to revolutionize the way students learn and understand complex concepts that usually arise in the STEM (Science, Mathematics, Engineering, and Technology) fields, as they inherently appeal to our highly developed and specialized visual system that effortlessly identifies patterns, trends, and outliers. Our paper presents a set of student-developed visualizations in strategically selected CS courses that enabled them to learn STEM related concepts in general (such as limits, differentiation, integration, and projectiles to name few), and CS concepts/algorithms in particular. In creating these visualization, the professor and the graduate assistants focused on incorporating into them a set of overarching themes that are effective and can be expanded to other fields. The themes were inspired by findings from a leading NSF Cutting Edge grant on teaching with visualization in a closely related field, although not one in STEM. The visualizations created were clear and simple; they are built on top of proven educational activities that were used in the past; the students’ feedback was a central component as the visualizations were built step by step; the visualizations defined the pre-conditions before which a student can watch or run them, so that context is well-defined and not lost; and finally, the visualizations were organized to reflect the mental organization that the student is creating. The paper will give details about the visualization algorithms, the criteria for their selection and inclusion in the curriculum, the students’ immediate feedback, and survey results taken by the students that contrast the traditional ways of teaching CS and STEM concepts vs. the use of the developed visualizations. The survey results, to be complete in December, 2016, will be analyzed with the hope of shedding light on whether visualizations make good tools for teaching, and if they have an effect on the rate (how quickly) of learning. Conclusions and recommendations will be presented. Keywords CS Education, Visualization, Animation, STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields, Image Processing, Software Engineering, Computer Vision.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Implementing a Challenge-Based Approach to Teaching Selected Courses in CS and Computational Sciences
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Challenge based learning/instruction (CBI) has been championed as an effective methodology to engage students in their own learning process, allowing them to bring real-life problems and projects that need to be solved. As The New Media Consortium eloquently puts it, " It [Challenge-based learning] calls for a new way of thinking about the role of the teacher, one in which he or she had to be comfortable as the students struggled and wrestled with a meaningful challenge, letting them choose their own path to understanding." The approach is even more challenging to implement in the SMT (Science, Mathematics, and Technology) fields at minority-serving institutions. To overcome these challenges, the author who is a Computer Science faculty with over twenty years industrial and academic experience in Computer Graphics and Imaging, was chosen to attend a set of extensive workshops, sponsored by the NSF (National Science Foundation), on how to effectively prepare course material and implement the learning method in strategically selected portions of any adopted course. Our paper describes in detail our efforts to implement Challenge based learning in the Computer Science curriculum in general, and Computer Graphics (CG) and Software Engineering (SWE) in particular. The effort is part of an NSF grant awarded to UT-Pan Am and UT Brownsville (both are now part of the newly merged university of UT-RGV). The CG/SWE courses were selected because of the initial high number of students’ enrollment in the class but the low retention rate by the class’s end. The paper will document/detail the efforts that have been taken in specific areas of the newly implemented courses. These include: 1. The process of identifying course major module objectives and module sub-objectives: In particular, those that are relevant to CBI implementation. 2. Identifying expected difficulties: What are the difficulties that students face when taking the course. 3. Real-world contexts: Why is the course an important part of the CS curriculum, and where can you find its applications. 4. Model of knowledge: What is the conceptual model for the course, including prerequisites, course dependencies, and course level. What concepts and techniques should be considered enduring understanding or important to do and know, or just worth being familiar with. 5. Assessment of learning: How do you change the traditional testing and assessment methods to make sure they include formative assessment (individual and group, in class and outside the class homework) as well as summative assessment. Data analysis and conclusions from the pilot project has been made public to benefit other faculty in CS and other SMT fields nationwide. Keywords Challenge based learning/instruction (CBI), Interdisciplinary Studies, Engineering, Computational Science, Computer Graphics, Software Engineering. SMT (Science, Mathematics, and Technology) fields at minority-serving institutions.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
In our continuous efforts to enhance the undergraduate curriculum in the Computer and Information Sciences department, we have created a new infrastructure networking and distributed processing lab (UTB/TSC-NDPL). The primary goal of this infrastructure is to enhance the existing curriculum in the undergraduate level by providing a state-of-the-art environment, isolated from the university campus network, in which Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) students can get hands on experience in areas such as Networking, Ad Hoc Computing, Wireless and Mobile Networking, Operating Systems, Image and Video Processing, Computer Vision and Distributed Processing.

The involved faculty, joined by top selected students, went through three distinct phases in creating the networking and distributed processing lab (NDPL): design and setup, specification and implementation, and integration into CIS curriculum. The design phase of the project relates to setting up the physical and logical topology of the network. We enclose a copy of the final design adopted as an appendix. The implementation phase relates to the choices of the equipment purchased and the different factors that influenced these choices as well as their overall role in the lab. As the design and implementation phases were completed, the CIS faculty created a new set of courses and lab modules to take advantage of the NDPL. Some new courses were created after the completion of the lab that include Internet/Intranet Server, Internet Communications, and Web Sever Support and Maintenance. Additionally, many lab modules were created to support current and existing courses and to improve research related to NDPL. These lab modules range from simple network setup and configuration to more advanced topics such as firewalls, streaming media, parallel computing, and distributed processing. The paper describes in detail the lab modules and how they relate to different competencies and course objectives set up by the department and based on accreditation authorities in the field. Since its inception and based on enrollment figures NDPL has played a vital role as a catalyst in retaining students in CS/CIS by allowing them to create and work in realistic real-world environments. Such unprecedented exposure is facilitating certification and licensure and is increasing the students’ competitiveness in the job market as well as preparing them for graduate studies in Science and Engineering should they choose to pursue that avenue.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
The Computer Science/Computer Information Systems (CS/CIS) Department at The University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB) has improved its curriculum by including parallel computing topics based on a computing and networking laboratory (CNL)1. Built around a 24-node distributed Beowulf2,3 supercomputer, the main goal of CNL is to enhance the understanding of parallel computing principles in key courses of the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science (BS-CS) degree, the two-year Associate in Applied Science in Computer Information Systems (AAS-CIS), and the four-year Bachelor of Applied Technology in Computer Information Systems Technology (BAT-CIST).

The strategy has been to use this supercomputer as the main instrument to infuse concepts and principles into targeted courses by creating a set of laboratory modules and capstone projects. Such project framework in CS education is strongly emphasized in the ACM/IEEE-CS curricula model4. CNL has aided in motivating the students by engaging them in integrating distributed computing and networking concepts into their course work through laboratory modules and capstone projects.

There are benefits in joining the practice and theory of different computer science areas via an integrated laboratory environment such as the one provided by CNL. First, it is easier to develop laboratory modules that help students to put different theoretical concepts together5,6. Second, an integrated laboratory is a low-cost solution compared to developing separate physical laboratories to serve different areas of computer science.

The laboratory has proved to be a dynamic educational tool for providing in depth understanding of essential concepts by incorporating state-of-the-art technologies into the curricula. This has allowed educators to keep on developing new laboratory modules for enriching their courses. In addition to currently implemented modules in areas like networking, databases and operating systems, new modules in areas such as encryption, autonomous intelligent systems, and web design and programming are planned to be developed, for example.

After being supported originally by NSF, the CNL project has reached maturity and it is now institutionalized. This paper details the rationale, scope and achievements of the project.
